## Theme: `theme_talkboy()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_talkboy()`, built from the Deluxe Talkboy cassette recorder: a dark walnut background, a silver frame and panel, button blue marks, and a Brush Script title.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a numeric (continuous) variable**
:::

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1999)
talkboy_clips <- tibble(
  clip_id = 1:300,
  seconds = round(rgamma(n = 300, shape = 4, rate = 0.5), 1)
)
labs_freqpoly <- labs(
  title = "Talkboy",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Length of 300 recorded messages",
  x = "Message length (seconds)")
ggp2_freqpoly <- ggplot(data = talkboy_clips,
      aes(x = seconds)) +
    geom_freqpoly()
ggp2_freqpoly +
  labs_freqpoly
```

::::

## Description

A frequency polygon is a plot that displays data distributions using points connected by straight lines. It's similar to a histogram but is more commonly used to compare data across multiple sets. A legend is often included to differentiate between various data sets. Frequency polygons are used to assess [symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_probability_distribution) and [skewness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness).

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

Install packages.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_freq_poly
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

::: {.column-margin}

![The Talkboy from *Home Alone 2* (from [`r/nostalgia`](https://www.reddit.com/r/nostalgia/comments/ebg2co/the_talkboy_recorder_from_home_alone/))](www/talkboy.jpg){fig-align="center" width="70%" height="70%"}

:::

The [Talkboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talkboy) was the handheld cassette recorder Kevin used in [*Home Alone 2* (1992)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0104431/), and Tiger Electronics sold the real thing that Christmas.[^deluxe]

We'll simulate 300 messages recorded on a Talkboy with `rgamma()`, rounding each message length to a tenth of a second. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 300 messages every time you run the code below.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_freq_poly
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1999) # same 300 clips every time the code runs
talkboy_clips <- tibble(
  clip_id = 1:300, # 300 different recordings, one row each
  seconds = round(
    rgamma(
      n = 300, 
     shape = 4, # clip lengths average 8 seconds (with a long right tail)
     rate = 0.5), 
    1 # one decimal place
    )
)
glimpse(talkboy_clips)
```
:::

## Distribution

If you ever handed a kid a tape recorder, you already know the shape of this distribution. Most messages last under 12 seconds, but every so often someone rambles on for 15 or 20. Those long messages stretch the right side of the distribution into a long tail, which makes it [right skewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness). Below we'll move from the numbers, to a picture, to the formula.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first ten messages.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: concrete_values_freq_poly
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(talkboy_clips$seconds, 10)
```
:::

Most of these are under 12 seconds, but one (14.5) runs much longer. Long messages like this pull the mean up, while the median (the middle message) barely moves. Comparing the two is a quick way to check for skew.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: concrete_summary_freq_poly
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
talkboy_clips |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(seconds),
    median = median(seconds))
```
:::

The mean is larger than the median, so more than half of the messages are shorter than the mean. We can count them by splitting the messages at the mean (about `r round(mean(talkboy_clips$seconds), 1)` seconds).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: concrete_counts_freq_poly
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
talkboy_split <- talkboy_clips |>
  mutate(speed = if_else(seconds < mean(seconds),
    "shorter than the mean", "the mean or longer"),
    speed = factor(speed,
      levels = c("shorter than the mean", "the mean or longer"))) |>
  count(speed)
talkboy_split
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

A bar model shows the split as two parts of one whole. If the distribution were symmetric, the two parts would be about the same size. Here the short messages take up the bigger part of the bar.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pictorial_bar_model_freq_poly
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| fig-asp: 0.45
ggplot(data = talkboy_split,
    aes(x = n, y = "300 messages", fill = speed)) +
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE),
    color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white",
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Number of messages", y = NULL,
    fill = "Message length")
```
:::

The frequency polygon below shows the same imbalance as a line. The dashed line marks the median and the solid line marks the mean. The tallest points sit at or left of the median, and the long tail trails off to the right, past the mean.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pictorial_freq_poly
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
ggplot(data = talkboy_clips,
    aes(x = seconds)) +
  geom_freqpoly() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(talkboy_clips$seconds),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "#1E1012") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(talkboy_clips$seconds),
    color = "#1E1012") +
  labs(x = "Message length (seconds)")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

The `rgamma()` call that created the data is a single statement:

$$
X \sim \text{Gamma}(k = 4, \lambda = 0.5)
$$

The [gamma distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_distribution) has two parameters. The shape ($k$) controls how lopsided the polygon is, and the rate ($\lambda$) controls how far it stretches along the `x` axis. From these two numbers we can calculate the mean ($k / \lambda = 8$ seconds), the peak ($(k - 1) / \lambda = 6$ seconds), and the standard deviation ($\sqrt{k} / \lambda = 4$ seconds). The peak comes before the mean, which is what right skew looks like in a formula.

Our simulated messages come close: the mean is `r round(mean(talkboy_clips$seconds), 1)` seconds and the standard deviation is `r round(sd(talkboy_clips$seconds), 1)` seconds. Try raising `shape` in `rgamma()` and the polygon becomes more symmetric. A gamma distribution with a large shape looks a lot like the normal distribution from @sec-histograms.


## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::


1. Create labels with `labs()`

2. Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

3. Map `seconds` to the `x` axis

4. Add the `geom_freqpoly()` layer


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_freq_poly
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
labs_freqpoly <- labs(
  title = "Talkboy",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Length of 300 recorded messages",
  x = "Message length (seconds)")
ggp2_freqpoly <- ggplot(data = talkboy_clips,
      aes(x = seconds)) +
    geom_freqpoly()
ggp2_freqpoly +
  labs_freqpoly
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_freq_poly
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_freqpoly <- labs(
  title = "Talkboy",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Length of 300 recorded messages",
  x = "Message length (seconds)")
ggp2_freqpoly <- ggplot(data = talkboy_clips,
      aes(x = seconds)) +
    geom_freqpoly()
ggp2_freqpoly +
  labs_freqpoly
```


Experiment to see how many `bins` fit your variable’s distribution.

```{r}
#| label: bins_freq_poly
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: show
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| layout-nrow: 1


ggp2_freqpoly_bins45 <- ggplot(data = talkboy_clips,
     aes(x = seconds)) +
     geom_freqpoly(bins = 45)

ggp2_freqpoly_bins45 +
  labs_freqpoly

ggp2_freqpoly_bins15 <- ggplot(data = talkboy_clips,
     aes(x = seconds)) +
     geom_freqpoly(bins = 15)

ggp2_freqpoly_bins15 +
  labs_freqpoly
```

[^deluxe]: Tiger Electronics sold the first Talkboy in 1992 and the Deluxe Talkboy, with the voice changer from the film, in April 1993.
